items.stem: Keynesian economic theory would assert that
options: (A) government interference in economics for the purpose of remedying a depression will only make matters worse
(B) the way to avoid an economic depression is for people to start saving a high percentage of their incomes as soon as the economy takes a downturn
(C) economic depressions worsen when individuals buy what they cannot comfortably afford
(D) lavish spending during an economic depression should be encouraged
items.explanation: Economist John Maynard Keynes theorized that a depression is the result of a vicious cycle: an economic downturn causes people to become anxious and reluctant to spend money, which leads businesses to fail and the economy to worsen, which leads to even greater anxiety and reluctance to spend money, which exacerbates the economic situation, etc. The way to stop the cycle and improve the economy is, perhaps counterintuitively, for people to spend money freely during times of hardship. The government can facilitate this process by providing its citizens with funds, whether through jobs or handouts, which they will presumably spend and thereby stimulate the economy. Roosevelt’s policies during the Great Depression were based on Keynesian economics.

option_explanations.A: That is the classical laissez-faire view Keynes argued against. Keynes held that government must intervene in a depression, not stand aside.
option_explanations.B: Keynes argued the opposite: when everyone saves during a downturn, demand collapses further (the paradox of thrift). Spending, not saving, breaks the cycle.
option_explanations.C: Keynes did not moralize about consumers buying what they cannot afford. His theory is about total (aggregate) demand in the economy, not about personal spending virtue.
option_explanations.D: Keynes theorized that depressions feed on collapsing demand: fear makes people stop spending, businesses fail, and the spiral deepens. The cure is spending — including lavish government spending, even at a deficit — to restore demand.

items.stem: Following the Spanish–American War and the acquisition of territory overseas, in a series of cases known as the Insular Cases, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that
options: (A) natives living on American soil abroad were guaranteed the same rights and privileges as U.S. citizens living within the continental United States
(B) colonial subjects within the American Empire were not entitled to the rights guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution
(C) “the Constitution follows the flag”
(D) Congress must relinquish control of these overseas possessions and honor their right of self-determination
items.explanation: As a result of winning the Spanish–American War in 1898, the United States acquired Guam, Puerto Rico, the Philippines, and for all intents and purposes, Cuba. (Although we had claimed we had no interest in acquiring Cuba and could empathize with its colonial status, having once been a colony ourselves, the Platt Amendment rendered the island a virtual colony of the United States.) The situation in the Philippines created intense debate between business interests that saw the enormous economic benefits to acquiring “stepping stones” to profitable Chinese trade, and those Americans who believed having colonies contradicted our fundamental democratic principles. Once we acquired overseas possessions, a question arose as to the rights and privileges of the Native peoples living within the American Empire. In a series of Supreme Court cases known as the Insular Cases, the Court ruled that the “Constitution did not follow the flag,” and thus, colonial subjects were not entitled to the same rights as U.S. citizens living at home or abroad.

option_explanations.A: The Court ruled the opposite: people in the newly acquired territories were not guaranteed the same constitutional rights as residents of the states.
option_explanations.B: In the Insular Cases (1901) the Court held that the Constitution does not fully apply to 'unincorporated' territories like Puerto Rico and the Philippines, so colonial subjects were not entitled to full constitutional rights.
option_explanations.C: 'The Constitution follows the flag' was the argument the Court rejected. The Insular Cases held that it does not automatically follow American sovereignty overseas.
option_explanations.D: The Court did not order Congress to give up the possessions or grant them self-determination. It upheld continued American control while withholding full constitutional protections.

items.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the contents of the Zimmermann telegram, which was intercepted in 1917?
options: (A) Germany offered Mexico an alliance and help regaining land lost in the Mexican Cession if Mexico attacked the United States
(B) A British spy alerted the world to the existence of mass extermination camps in German-held territories.
(C) The United States assured the British that it would join the war in Europe if the war were to continue for another year.
(D) The owner of the Boston Red Sox revealed a plan to sell star player Babe Ruth to the New York Yankees for a large amount of cash.
items.explanation: This is a straight recall question. You either know what the Zimmermann telegram is or you don’t. If you know it, you’re going to get this question right. If you don’t, use Process of Elimination to get rid of anachronistic answers, as in (B), or answers that seem un-AP-like because they don’t reinforce important themes of U.S. history, as in (D). You should know, however, that the Zimmermann telegram was one of the reasons the United States entered World War I.

option_explanations.A: In the intercepted 1917 telegram, German foreign minister Zimmermann offered Mexico a military alliance: if the United States entered World War I, Mexico should attack it and would be rewarded with the territory lost in the 1848 Mexican Cession (Texas, New Mexico, Arizona). Its publication helped push the U.S. into the war.
option_explanations.B: Mass extermination camps belong to World War II and the Holocaust, not to World War I. This is anachronistic by a generation.
option_explanations.C: The telegram ran the other way: it was from Germany to Mexico, intercepted and decoded by the British. It contained no American assurance to Britain.
option_explanations.D: Babe Ruth's sale to the Yankees (1919-20) is baseball history, unrelated to World War I diplomacy.

items.stem: Wilson’s Fourteen Points plan for peace after World War I included all of the following EXCEPT
options: (A) promotion of universal self-determination
(B) lower tariffs to promote free trade
(C) repayment of all Allied war expenses by Germany
(D) across-the-board arms reductions
items.explanation: In the aftermath of World War I, President Wilson favored a peace that would promote openness in international affairs, free trade, and diplomacy. He also sought universal arms reductions and a mechanism for enforcing world peace, which was to be achieved through the League of Nations. He did not seek a punitive treaty that forced Germany to pay heavy reparations; the European allies, however, insisted. Wilson was able to negotiate very little of his Fourteen Points plan, but he remained optimistic that the League of Nations would eventually broker a fairer postwar peace. Unfortunately, Wilson’s hopes were never realized.

option_explanations.A: Universal self-determination for peoples was central to the Fourteen Points — not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Removing trade barriers and lowering tariffs was part of Wilson's vision of free trade — not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Wilson did not want a punitive peace. He opposed forcing Germany to pay heavy reparations; the European Allies imposed them anyway in the Treaty of Versailles.
option_explanations.D: Across-the-board arms reductions were part of the Fourteen Points — not the exception.

items.stem: All of the following can be seen as clashes between traditional and modern culture during the Post–World War I Era EXCEPT
options: (A) the rise of the Ku Klux Klan
(B) the Teapot Dome Scandal
(C) the Scopes Monkey Trial
(D) the Emergency Quota Act
items.explanation: The Ku Klux Klan evoked the execrable southern traditions of racism and physical intimidation against the modern drive for expanded civil rights. The Scopes Monkey Trial pitted religion against the modern notion of evolution. The Emergency Quota Act was passed to check immigration from non-western European countries; its champions felt the nation’s Western European traditions were threatened by immigrants from Southern Europe, Eastern Europe, South America, and Asia. The Teapot Dome Scandal, on the other hand, was just an example of good old-fashioned political corruption.

option_explanations.A: The 1920s Klan revival fused old-style racism and intimidation with resistance to the modern expansion of civil rights — a genuine traditional-vs.-modern clash, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: The Teapot Dome Scandal was straightforward political corruption — Harding administration officials taking bribes for naval oil leases. It was not a clash of traditional and modern culture, so it is the exception.
option_explanations.C: The Scopes Monkey Trial (1925) pitted religious traditionalism against the modern science of evolution — a genuine culture clash, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: The Emergency Quota Act (1921) reflected nativist traditionalism pushing back against modern immigration from southern and eastern Europe — a genuine culture clash, not the exception.

items.stem: Which of the following was NOT a New Deal policy?
options: (A) Federal insurance for banks in order to ensure the confidence of depositors
(B) Stricter laws against unionizing in order to prevent loss of income due to strikes
(C) Payments to farmers who agreed to substantially reduce production in order to stabilize prices
(D) Government regulation of the stock market in order to protect investors
items.explanation: Roosevelt adopted a pro-union stance regarding the New Deal, believing that the right to collective bargaining was critical to ensuring decent wages for workers. Americans would have more money to spend if they were adequately paid, and increased spending would benefit the economy.

option_explanations.A: Federal deposit insurance was a New Deal policy: the FDIC (1933) insured bank deposits to restore depositor confidence — not the exception.
option_explanations.B: The New Deal was pro-union, not anti-union. Roosevelt backed collective bargaining (Wagner Act, 1935), so stricter laws against unionizing are the opposite of New Deal policy — this is the exception.
option_explanations.C: Paying farmers to cut production was a New Deal policy: the Agricultural Adjustment Act (1933) paid farmers to reduce output and stabilize prices — not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Regulating the stock market was a New Deal policy: the Securities and Exchange Commission (1934) was created to protect investors — not the exception.
